title: Dermatomes & Sensory Testing
keywords: dermatome dermatomes sensation sensory testing light touch pinprick key sensory points asia isncsci
summary: Find every key sensory point from C2 to S4–S5, test light touch and pinprick properly, and read sensory patterns — root, nerve, polyneuropathy or cord.
ur: Har dermatome ka key sensory point dhoondna, light touch aur pinprick sahi tareeqe se test karna, aur sensory pattern se lesion samajhna.

sources.title: ASIA — International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI, 2019 revision)

goals.beginner: Point to every key sensory point from C2 to S4–S5.
goals.intermediate: Test light touch and pinprick correctly and score them.
goals.advanced: Tell root, nerve, polyneuropathy and cord patterns apart.
goals.expert: Find the sensory level, recognise red flags and pass OSCE stations.

concepts.title: What is a dermatome?
concepts.body: A **dermatome** is the strip of skin supplied by **one spinal nerve root**. A **peripheral nerve field** is the skin supplied by one named nerve (which carries fibres from several roots). Knowing both lets you tell a root problem from a nerve problem.
concepts.ur: Dermatome = ek spinal root ki skin. Peripheral nerve ka area different hota hai kyunke ek nerve mein kai roots hoti hain.

concepts.title: Key sensory points
concepts.body: Dermatomes overlap, so the ISNCSCI standard uses one **key sensory point** per level — a spot that reliably belongs to that root. Test these points instead of guessing at borders.
bullets: **L4** medial malleolus · **L5** dorsum of foot · **S1** lateral heel
concepts.ur: Har level ka ek fixed key point hai — thumb C6, middle finger C7, little finger C8, umbilicus T10.

concepts.title: Memory tricks that stick
concepts.body: Hold your hand up: thumb and index make a **6** (C6); the middle finger is **7**; the little finger is **8**. T10 is the belly-bu**TTON**. L4 is on the floor (medial malleolus); S1 is the **side** of the foot you stand on.

concepts.title: Testing light touch and pinprick
concepts.body: Show the sensation on the face first (the normal reference). Then, with the patient's eyes closed, test each key point and compare with the face and the other side.
bullets: **Light touch**: a wisp of cotton wool — “Does it feel the same as on your face?”
**Pinprick**: a clean safety pin — “Sharp or dull?” (alternate sharp and dull randomly).
Score **2** normal, **1** altered (reduced or increased), **0** absent.
Never use a needle that breaks the skin; discard single-use pins.
concepts.ur: Pehle face par demonstrate karein, phir eyes band karwa ke har point test karein aur doosri side se compare karein.

concepts.title: Which pathway are you testing?
concepts.body: Different modalities travel in different tracts — that's why testing more than one helps localise a lesion.

head: Modality
Pathway
Crosses
rows: In the cord, near the level of entry
Both dorsal columns and anterior spinothalamic
Vibration (128 Hz fork), joint position sense

concepts.title: Read the pattern
concepts.body: The shape of the sensory change points to the lesion.

head: Pattern
Think of
rows: Area of one named nerve (e.g. lateral 3½ fingers, palm side)
Peripheral nerve (e.g. median at the wrist)
Pain/temperature lost on one side, proprioception on the other

concepts.title: ISNCSCI sensory scoring
concepts.body: Each of the 28 key points on each side is scored 0–2 for light touch and for pinprick — a maximum of **112 per modality**. The **sensory level** is the most caudal level with normal (2) light touch **and** pinprick on that side.

concepts.title: Never skip S3–S5
concepts.body: Ask about saddle numbness and bladder or bowel change in every patient with back pain and leg symptoms. Reduced perianal sensation with urinary retention or incontinence is **cauda equina syndrome** — same-day emergency referral. In spinal cord injury, preserved **S4–S5** sensation (sacral sparing) means the injury is incomplete — a better prognosis.
concepts.ur: Back pain ke saath saddle numbness ya bladder/bowel mein change = emergency (cauda equina). Foran refer karein.

concepts.title: Overlap, variation and diabetes screening
concepts.body: Adjacent dermatomes overlap, so a single-root lesion often gives a smaller area of loss than the map suggests — and maps differ between textbooks. For diabetic feet, use a **10 g monofilament** at standard sites on the sole: inability to feel it signals loss of protective sensation and ulcer risk.

questions.prompt: A dermatome is the skin supplied by…
options: One muscle
One named peripheral nerve
One spinal nerve root
One spinal cord tract
questions.explain: Dermatome = one root; a peripheral nerve field carries fibres from several roots.

questions.prompt: Which level does the umbilicus mark?
options: T4
L1
questions.explain: T10 = belly button.

questions.prompt: The key sensory point for C6 is…
options: The thumb
The medial elbow
The middle finger
The little finger
questions.explain: C6 = thumb (dorsal proximal phalanx).

questions.prompt: The lateral heel tests…
options: L4
L5
S1
S3
questions.explain: S1 = lateral heel/little-toe side of the foot.

questions.prompt: Why use key sensory points?
options: Dermatomes overlap — one reliable point per level avoids guessing at borders
They are faster to draw
They test muscles
They only matter in children
questions.explain: Key points are reliably supplied by a single root.

questions.prompt: Before testing light touch, you should first…
options: Ask the patient to look at the limb
Apply the pin firmly to break the skin
Demonstrate the normal sensation on the face
Test the most painful area
questions.explain: The face gives the patient a 'normal' reference.

questions.prompt: In ISNCSCI, a light-touch score of 1 means…
options: Altered (reduced or increased) sensation
Normal
Not tested
Absent
questions.explain: 0 absent · 1 altered · 2 normal.

questions.prompt: Pinprick and temperature travel in the…
options: Dorsal columns
Corticospinal tract
Spinocerebellar tract
Spinothalamic tract
questions.explain: Pain and temperature = spinothalamic.

questions.prompt: Vibration is tested with…
options: A safety pin
A 512 Hz fork
A 128 Hz tuning fork
Cotton wool
questions.explain: 128 Hz for vibration sense (512 Hz is for hearing).

questions.prompt: During pinprick testing the patient's eyes should be…
options: Open and watching
Closed
It doesn't matter
Covered only for the face
questions.explain: Closed eyes prevent visual cueing.

questions.prompt: Proprioception (joint position sense) is tested by…
options: Moving the big toe or finger up/down by its sides with the patient's eyes closed
Using a 10 g monofilament
Asking the patient to stand on one leg
Pressing the nail bed
questions.explain: Hold the digit by its sides so pressure gives no clue to direction.

questions.prompt: When mapping an area of numbness, move the stimulus…
options: From normal skin into the abnormal area only once
Along the spine only
Randomly
From the abnormal area towards normal skin
questions.explain: Abnormal → normal gives a sharper border (the patient reports when it becomes normal).

questions.prompt: Light touch should be tested with…
options: Cotton wool dabbed, not stroked
A firm drag of a pin
The examiner's fingertip pressed hard
A tuning fork
questions.explain: Stroking stimulates hair and tickle fibres; dab the cotton wool.

questions.prompt: Two-point discrimination on the fingertip is normally about…
options: Under 0.5 mm
2–5 mm
40 mm
questions.explain: Fingertips are highly innervated; values over ~6 mm are abnormal.

questions.prompt: Which dermatome covers the nipple line?
options: T1
T4
T7
questions.explain: T4 = nipple, T6 = xiphoid, T10 = umbilicus.

questions.prompt: Symmetrical numbness of both feet and hands, distal more than proximal, suggests…
options: Median nerve lesion
Polyneuropathy
L5 radiculopathy
Cord lesion at T10
questions.explain: Glove-and-stocking = length-dependent polyneuropathy (e.g. diabetes).

questions.prompt: Loss of pinprick below the umbilicus on both sides suggests…
options: Peripheral neuropathy
Femoral nerve lesions
A spinal cord lesion around T10
Bilateral L5 radiculopathy
questions.explain: A horizontal sensory level points to the cord.

questions.prompt: The ISNCSCI sensory level is…
options: The first abnormal level
The level of the fracture on imaging
The motor level
The most caudal level with normal light touch AND pinprick
questions.explain: Most caudal fully normal level for both modalities.

questions.prompt: Maximum ISNCSCI light-touch score?
questions.explain: 28 key points × 2 points × 2 sides = 112.

questions.prompt: Numbness of the palmar thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger only suggests…
options: Ulnar nerve
Median nerve (e.g. carpal tunnel)
C6 root
C8 root
questions.explain: That is the median nerve's palmar field, not a dermatome.

questions.case: Low back pain with bilateral sciatica; new difficulty passing urine and numbness 'where I sit'.
questions.prompt: What do you do?
options: Test reflexes next visit
Arrange same-day emergency assessment for cauda equina syndrome
Book physiotherapy next week
Give a home exercise sheet
questions.explain: Saddle anaesthesia + urinary change = emergency.

questions.case: Spinal cord injury: no motor function below T6, but the patient feels light touch around the anus (S4–S5).
questions.prompt: What does this mean?
options: The sensory level is S4
Testing error — ignore it
The injury is incomplete (sacral sparing) — better prognosis
The injury is complete
questions.explain: Any preserved S4–S5 function makes the injury incomplete.

questions.case: After a stab wound: right leg weak with loss of vibration and position sense; left leg has lost pain and temperature below T10.
questions.prompt: Which lesion?
options: Cauda equina
Polyneuropathy
Left hemicord lesion
Right hemicord (Brown-Séquard) lesion
questions.explain: Ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss, contralateral spinothalamic loss.

questions.prompt: Diabetic foot screening uses…
options: A 10 g monofilament at standard sole sites
A reflex hammer
Two-point discrimination on the back
A goniometer
questions.explain: Inability to feel the 10 g monofilament = loss of protective sensation.

questions.case: Numb dorsum of the foot, weak EHL and weak hip abduction.
questions.prompt: Most likely level?
options: S1 root
L3 root
L5 root
Common fibular nerve
questions.explain: Hip abductor weakness puts the lesion at the L5 root, not the fibular nerve.

questions.case: Neck pain; numbness of the middle finger only; weak elbow extension; reduced triceps reflex.
questions.prompt: Most likely level?
options: C8 root
Radial nerve at the spiral groove
C7 root
C6 root
questions.explain: Middle finger + triceps weakness + triceps reflex = C7 (the commonest cervical radiculopathy).

questions.case: Burning numbness of the anterolateral thigh only; no weakness; reflexes normal; tight belt and recent weight gain.
questions.prompt: Most likely cause?
options: L3 radiculopathy
Femoral nerve lesion
Cauda equina syndrome
Meralgia paraesthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve)
questions.explain: A purely sensory patch with no motor or reflex change fits a cutaneous nerve, not a root.

questions.case: Loss of pain and temperature across both shoulders and arms ('cape' distribution) with preserved light touch.
questions.prompt: Which lesion?
options: Central cord lesion such as syringomyelia
Brown-Séquard syndrome
Bilateral C5 radiculopathy
Peripheral polyneuropathy
questions.explain: Crossing spinothalamic fibres are damaged centrally; dorsal columns are spared (dissociated sensory loss).

questions.case: Ulnar-side hand numbness that extends up the medial forearm; weak finger abduction and thumb flexion.
questions.prompt: C8 root or ulnar nerve?
options: Median nerve
C8 root — the medial forearm (medial antebrachial cutaneous) is not ulnar territory
Ulnar nerve at the elbow
Ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal
questions.explain: Sensory loss above the wrist on the medial forearm and weak FPL (median, C8) point to the root.

stations.title: Upper-limb sensory screen (C5–T1)
stations.scenario: A 40-year-old with neck pain and tingling in the right hand. Test light touch and pinprick from C5 to T1 and report.
tasks: Explain and demonstrate on the face.
Test the five key points on both sides.
checklist: Demonstrates light touch and pinprick on the face as the reference
Tests C5 lateral elbow, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial elbow
Compares right and left at each point
Scores 0/1/2 and identifies a dermatomal pattern
Suggests matching myotome and reflex tests

stations.title: Cauda equina screen
stations.scenario: A patient with acute low back pain and bilateral leg pain. Screen for cauda equina syndrome and explain your decision.
tasks: Explain how saddle sensation is tested.
checklist: Asks about urinary retention, incontinence or reduced sensation passing urine
Asks about bowel and sexual dysfunction
Asks about bilateral or progressive leg weakness/numbness
Explains S3–S5 sensory testing with consent and a chaperone
States same-day emergency referral if any red flag is present

stations.title: Lower-limb sensory screen (L2–S2)
stations.scenario: A patient with left-sided sciatica. Test lower-limb dermatomes and identify the most likely root.
tasks: Test the key points L2–S2 on both sides.
checklist: Tests L2 anterior thigh, L3 medial knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral heel, S2 popliteal fossa
Names the root matching the altered point
Links to myotome (e.g. L5 = EHL) and reflex (S1 = Achilles)
Demonstrates the stimulus on the face first and keeps the patient's eyes closed
Screens saddle (S3–S5) sensation and asks about bladder/bowel change

cards.front: A dermatome is the skin supplied by…
cards.back: One spinal nerve root. Dermatome = one root; a peripheral nerve field carries fibres from several roots.

cards.front: Which level does the umbilicus mark?
cards.back: T10. T10 = belly button.

cards.front: The key sensory point for C6 is…
cards.back: The thumb. C6 = thumb (dorsal proximal phalanx).

cards.front: The lateral heel tests…
cards.back: S1. S1 = lateral heel/little-toe side of the foot.

cards.front: Why use key sensory points?
cards.back: Dermatomes overlap — one reliable point per level avoids guessing at borders. Key points are reliably supplied by a single root.

cards.front: Before testing light touch, you should first…
cards.back: Demonstrate the normal sensation on the face. The face gives the patient a 'normal' reference.

cards.front: In ISNCSCI, a light-touch score of 1 means…
cards.back: Altered (reduced or increased) sensation. 0 absent · 1 altered · 2 normal.

cards.front: Pinprick and temperature travel in the…
cards.back: Spinothalamic tract. Pain and temperature = spinothalamic.

cards.front: Vibration is tested with…
cards.back: A 128 Hz tuning fork. 128 Hz for vibration sense (512 Hz is for hearing).

cards.front: During pinprick testing the patient's eyes should be…
cards.back: Closed. Closed eyes prevent visual cueing.

cards.front: Proprioception (joint position sense) is tested by…
cards.back: Moving the big toe or finger up/down by its sides with the patient's eyes closed. Hold the digit by its sides so pressure gives no clue to direction.

cards.front: When mapping an area of numbness, move the stimulus…
cards.back: From the abnormal area towards normal skin. Abnormal → normal gives a sharper border (the patient reports when it becomes normal).

cards.front: Light touch should be tested with…
cards.back: Cotton wool dabbed, not stroked. Stroking stimulates hair and tickle fibres; dab the cotton wool.

cards.front: Two-point discrimination on the fingertip is normally about…
cards.back: 2–5 mm. Fingertips are highly innervated; values over ~6 mm are abnormal.

cards.front: Which dermatome covers the nipple line?
cards.back: T4. T4 = nipple, T6 = xiphoid, T10 = umbilicus.

cards.front: Symmetrical numbness of both feet and hands, distal more than proximal, suggests…
cards.back: Polyneuropathy. Glove-and-stocking = length-dependent polyneuropathy (e.g. diabetes).

cards.front: Loss of pinprick below the umbilicus on both sides suggests…
cards.back: A spinal cord lesion around T10. A horizontal sensory level points to the cord.

cards.front: The ISNCSCI sensory level is…
cards.back: The most caudal level with normal light touch AND pinprick. Most caudal fully normal level for both modalities.

cards.front: Maximum ISNCSCI light-touch score?
cards.back: 112. 28 key points × 2 points × 2 sides = 112.

cards.front: Numbness of the palmar thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger only suggests…
cards.back: Median nerve (e.g. carpal tunnel). That is the median nerve's palmar field, not a dermatome.

cards.front: Low back pain with bilateral sciatica; new difficulty passing urine and numbness 'where I sit'. — What do you do?
cards.back: Arrange same-day emergency assessment for cauda equina syndrome. Saddle anaesthesia + urinary change = emergency.

cards.front: Spinal cord injury: no motor function below T6, but the patient feels light touch around the anus (S4–S5). — What does this mean?
cards.back: The injury is incomplete (sacral sparing) — better prognosis. Any preserved S4–S5 function makes the injury incomplete.

cards.front: After a stab wound: right leg weak with loss of vibration and position sense; left leg has lost pain and temperature below T10. — Which lesion?
cards.back: Right hemicord (Brown-Séquard) lesion. Ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss, contralateral spinothalamic loss.

cards.front: Diabetic foot screening uses…
cards.back: A 10 g monofilament at standard sole sites. Inability to feel the 10 g monofilament = loss of protective sensation.

cards.front: Numb dorsum of the foot, weak EHL and weak hip abduction. — Most likely level?
cards.back: L5 root. Hip abductor weakness puts the lesion at the L5 root, not the fibular nerve.

cards.front: Neck pain; numbness of the middle finger only; weak elbow extension; reduced triceps reflex. — Most likely level?
cards.back: C7 root. Middle finger + triceps weakness + triceps reflex = C7 (the commonest cervical radiculopathy).

cards.front: Burning numbness of the anterolateral thigh only; no weakness; reflexes normal; tight belt and recent weight gain. — Most likely cause?
cards.back: Meralgia paraesthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve). A purely sensory patch with no motor or reflex change fits a cutaneous nerve, not a root.

cards.front: Loss of pain and temperature across both shoulders and arms ('cape' distribution) with preserved light touch. — Which lesion?
cards.back: Central cord lesion such as syringomyelia. Crossing spinothalamic fibres are damaged centrally; dorsal columns are spared (dissociated sensory loss).

cards.front: Ulnar-side hand numbness that extends up the medial forearm; weak finger abduction and thumb flexion. — C8 root or ulnar nerve?
cards.back: C8 root — the medial forearm (medial antebrachial cutaneous) is not ulnar territory. Sensory loss above the wrist on the medial forearm and weak FPL (median, C8) point to the root.
